question.text: Identify the Incan ruler whom Pizarro seized and executed after demanding and receiving a roomful of gold as ransom.
question.clue: He offered to fill a large room with gold and silver for his ransom, but the Spaniards didn't release him.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about the native peoples of the Americas.
swap.text: This civilization, with capital at Cuzco and another city at Macchu Picchu, was conquered by Francisco Pizarro.
swap.clue: Descendants of this empire's royalty included Garcilaso de la Vega, and this empire was sometimes named for the four administrative suyus that it was divided into.

question.leadin: Answer the following about indigenous peoples of South America.
question.text: The Quechua group, who share their name with the language of the Inca Empire, live in and around this mountain range in Peru, Ecuador, and Bolivia.
question.clue: A culture in this mountain range depicted a spider called the "Decapitator" and created a mummy known as the Lord of Sipan.

swap.text: Identify the Spaniard who conquered the Incan Empire.
swap.clue: This man received help from longtime partner Diego Almagro, but he was killed by Almagro's forces in the Battle of Las Salinas.

question.text: Paul Kosok discovered the Hummingbird, an earthwork built by these people indigenous to Peru. These people built the city of Cahuachi [ca-WA-chee] and used puquios to irrigate their crops.
question.clue: Paul Kosok and Maria Reiche (RAI-keh) mapped structures created by these people.

swap.leadin: The "trophy heads" collected by this culture featured a hole in the skull where a rope was threaded through.
swap.text: Name this culture who created geoglyphs in the shape of condors and hummingbirds in the desert, known as their namesake "lines."
swap.clue: This culture built the Cantalloc ("cahn-TAH-yoke")Aqueducts, exemplifying the corkscrew entrances of their puquios ("poo-KEE-ohʼs").

question.leadin: This country is home to a Maoist cell called Shining Path, whose crackdown led to many human rights abuses by its ethnically Japanese president Alberto Fujimori in the 90s.
question.text: Name this country whose navy was beaten by nearby Chile in the War of the Pacific. This country just got back a trove of artifacts that Yale stole from Machu Picchu.
question.clue: That culture in this country was also responsible for creating a series of images called Lines near Palpa that are well-known geoglyphs.

swap.leadin: This culture built a network of roads along which messengers carried quantitative messages on lines of knotted string called quipu.
swap.text: Name this Quechua-speaking South American civilization with a capital at Cusco, which built Machu Picchu. Conquistadors led by Francisco Pizarro toppled this civilization.
swap.clue: This empire's language was Quechua, and these people built Machu Picchu.

question.leadin: In the 1860s, ships from this country sailed to Polynesia to abduct laborers through a practice known as "blackbirding"
question.text: Name this country that needed workers for its profitable guano mines. A president of Japanese ancestry fought against the Shining Path in this country.
question.clue: The Marxist Shining Path rebels fought against the government of this country, which became a dictatorship in the years following Alberto Fujimori's electoral victory over Mario Vargas Llosa.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about the Inca emperor Atahualpa.
swap.text: After the death of his father Huayna Capac, Atahualpa fought this brother for control of the Inca Empire. He was defeated and imprisoned after losses at Chimborazo and Quipaipan.
swap.clue: This Peruvian ship sank the Esmeralda before Chile captured it in the War of the Pacific. It took its name from an Incan noble who lost a civil war to his brother Atahualpa.

question.text: Conquistadors high off chivalric fantasies searched for this mythical city of gold inspired by Muisca folklore.
question.clue: During the first part of the journey in which Orellana travelled the length of the Amazon, a valley of Cinnamon and this place were the targets of Gonzalo Pizzaro.

swap.text: This conquistador captured and eventually executed the Incan leader Atahualpa [ah-tah-WAHL-pah] after the Battle of Cajamarca.
swap.clue: He led a band dubbed the "Famous 13" and gained over twenty tons of precious metals after setting up the "Ransom Room."

question.leadin: Original language term required. Before approaching a relay station, people with this job would sound a pututu shell to announce their presence.
question.text: Name these messengers who traversed the Qhapaq Nan ("KA-pak NYAN") to deliver messages in the form of knotted strings, or quipu ("KEE-poo").
question.clue: Quipus were often stored at stations known as tambos, where these messengers of the Inca would stop to relay information to other carriers.

swap.leadin: The former MIT student Lori Berenson was accused of collaborating with a modern organization named for this person.
swap.text: Identify this man who names a "Revolutionary Movement" led by Victor Campos. This Indigenous rebel, who took his name from a monarch executed at Vilcabamba, was defeated at the 1780 Battle of Sangarara.
swap.answerHtml: Túpac Amaru II [in place of “Túpac” accept Thupaq or Thupa or Topa; in place of “Amaru” accept Amaro; accept Túpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement; prompt on José Gabriel Condorcanqui by asking “what name did he adopt?”; prompt on MRTA]
swap.clue: This leader's revolt targeted the expansion of the alcabala and a system of forced mining labour called the mit'a.

question.leadin: These Chibcha-speaking people migrated to the Altiplano Cundiboyacense ["koon-di-boya-sen-say"] at some point between 1000 BCE and 500 CE and founded cities like Hunza and Bacata.
question.text: Name these people, who mined salt in large gacha pots and imported gold for tunjo figures of humans or animals at Guatavita.
question.clue: This confederation of Northern Andean tribes that was led by co-rulers called Zipa and Zaque. They were encountered by the Conquistador Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada after his expedition sailed up the Magdalena.

swap.leadin: According to one crackpot theory, these structures were built using medieval hot-air balloons.
swap.text: Name these massive desert drawings that have been hypothesized to represent constellations. Greenpeace activists managed to damage one shaped like a hummingbird in late 2014.
swap.answerHtml: Nazca Lines [accept Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa, accept Lineas de Nazca]
swap.clue: These things were damaged by Greenpeace activists wearing improper footwear as part of a 2014 protest.

question.text: The original "Maritime Foundations" theory was developed after the excavation of this site at the mouth of the Supe River that likely provided fish to Caral from the nearby ocean. This place is the type site of the Norte Chico.

swap.text: The Inca used mit'a ("MITT-ah") labor to construct the rope bridges which connected sections of this 25,000-mile-long system together.
swap.clue: Stations called tambos could be found along this system, which was known in one language as Qhapaq Nan.

question.leadin: This ruler exempted Quechua speakers from taxation.
question.text: Name this son of Viracocha who defeated the Chanca invasion of Cuzco. The sun temple Coricancha, and possibly Machu Picchu, were built by this ruler.
question.clue: This ruler, who legendarily subjugated the (+) Chanka people with stone warriors, organized his realm into four suyus.

swap.leadin: The Met holds a work made of this material with French lettering and scenes from Greek mythology, and a lliklla ("LEEK-l'yah") made of this material that imitates Spanish-style lattice motifs.
swap.text: Name this material used to make low-quality awasqa or high-quality qunpi ("COMB-pee"), decorated with tukapu motifs. A red llawt'u ("l'YAO-too") decorated the maskhaypacha, an imperial symbol made of this material.
swap.answerHtml: camelid wool [or millma or millwa or willma; accept camelid hair or camelid fur; accept fleece in place of “wool”; accept llama, alpaca, or vicuña in place of “camelid”; prompt on hair or fur; prompt on textile or fabric or clothing or p’achakuna by asking “made of what substance?”; prompt on cotton or utkhu by asking “what material is more commonly used?”; reject “rope” or “chord”]
